basics.name: CAD assembly joint datasets: Fusion 360 Gallery Assembly Dataset (with its JoinABLe joint subset, Autodesk Research), AutoMate (University of Washington with Adobe/Onshape data), and Assemble Them All (MIT CSAIL with Autodesk)
basics.url: https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/Fusion360GalleryDataset (Fusion 360 Gallery, including the Assembly and Assembly-Joint data); https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/JoinABLe (JoinABLe code); https://zenodo.org/records/7776208 (AutoMate dataset; code at https://github.com/deGravity/automate); https://github.com/yunshengtian/Assemble-Them-All (Assemble Them All code and dataset links). The github.com pages were read through their raw README files
basics.resource_type: GitHub repo or dataset (three related machine-learning research datasets of real CAD assemblies, where parts are connected by labelled joints, also called mates, plus code and papers)
basics.cost: Free (large downloads: Fusion 360 Assembly-Joint data 2.8 GB; AutoMate about 35 GB in total, most of it Parasolid and STEP geometry; Assemble Them All 5.4 MB to 778 MB per subset)
basics.license: Mixed. Fusion 360 Gallery Dataset: Autodesk's own licence, non-commercial research use only; you may not redistribute the whole dataset, only point people to the GitHub repo, and modified subsets must stay non-commercial. AutoMate dataset: CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication) on both Zenodo and Dryad, so its list of mate types and statistics can be reused freely, although the underlying part models came from public Onshape documents made by users [uncertain: whether the original designers' rights still apply]. Assemble Them All: code is MIT-licensed; its dataset is mostly modified from Fusion 360 Gallery, so the README tells users to follow the Fusion 360 Gallery licence. JoinABLe code: MIT. For the encyclopedia: linking is fine; do not copy Fusion 360 Gallery thumbnails or models onto a public site
basics.year: Fusion 360 Gallery Reconstruction dataset paper 2020 (arXiv 2010.02392); Assembly Dataset and JoinABLe first released with arXiv 2111.12772 in November 2021 (v2 April 2022; CVPR 2022); Fusion 360 licence updated 11/2021. AutoMate: arXiv 2105.12238 May 2021 (v2 October 2021), ACM Transactions on Graphics December 2021 (SIGGRAPH Asia 2021); dataset deposited on Zenodo and Dryad 27 March 2023. Assemble Them All: arXiv 2211.03977 November 2022, ACM TOG December 2022 (SIGGRAPH Asia 2022); README notes a dataset update in March 2024 (dataset_2403)
basics.access_barrier: none for the download links (no login). But using the data needs technical skills: 7z/zip archives of several GB, B-Rep files (.smt needs Autodesk Shape Manager/Fusion 360; Parasolid .x_t needs the commercial Parasolid kernel), and Python/conda code. STEP and OBJ versions can be opened in free tools such as FreeCAD
basics.image_license: Thumbnails (PNG) and README images fall under each project's terms: Fusion 360 Gallery thumbnails under the non-commercial research licence (which also makes the user responsible for copies of copyrighted images they create); AutoMate data under CC0; README GIFs in the Assemble Them All and JoinABLe repos have no separate image licence stated [uncertain]
basics.authority_level: academic peer-reviewed (CVPR 2022, ACM Transactions on Graphics / SIGGRAPH Asia 2021 and 2022), from Autodesk Research, MIT CSAIL, University of Washington and collaborators. The joint labels themselves are set by the original CAD designers (community), not by expert annotators

coverage.covers: Real designer-made CAD assemblies and the joints (mates) between their parts. Fusion 360 Gallery Assembly: 8,251 assemblies with 154,468 parts, each joint labelled with one of Fusion 360's 7 joint types (rigid, revolute, slider, cylindrical, pin-slot, planar, ball), plus motion limits and rest pose, contact surfaces and 24 recognised hole types (counterbore, countersunk, blind, through, tapered and so on). Its Assembly-Joint subset (used by JoinABLe): 19,156 joint sets with 32,148 joints between 23,029 parts. AutoMate: 255,211 assemblies, 451,967 unique parts and 1,292,016 unique mates scraped from public Onshape documents, labelled with Onshape's 8 mate types (frequencies among the paper's 541,635 unique mates: fastened 62.1%, revolute 12.7%, planar 11.8%, slider 5.3%, cylindrical 5.1%, parallel 1.8%, ball 0.6%, pin slot 0.5%), plus 'mate relations' that couple two mates (Onshape offers gear, rack-and-pinion, screw and linear relations). Assemble Them All: 12,970 physically valid assemblies (8,776 two-part, the rest 3 to 235 parts) with a small 24-assembly rotational subset (screws and nuts, puzzles, other twisting motions); it labels assembly paths and sequences, not joint types
coverage.organisation: Organised as data files by numeric or hashed ID, not for browsing: one JSON per assembly or joint set, with parts as B-Rep/STEP/OBJ files. Joint types are enum values (e.g. 'RevoluteJointType', 'FASTENED'). There are no human-readable pages, categories or search. For someone who does not know the terms it does not work at all as a reference; its value is the compact, standard list of joint types and the statistics of how often each is used
coverage.scope_match: low. It is about generic CAD joint TYPES by degrees of freedom (rigid, hinge, slider and so on), which are the building-block motions every connection has, not the unusual or clever connection and mechanism types the encyclopedia wants. It does not name snap fits, ratchets, torque limiters, latches or adhesives. Useful mainly as a sanity check for a 'how does it move' filter and for real-world frequency data
coverage.taxonomy_used: CAD kinematic joint (mate) types classified by degrees of freedom (DOF, the ways a part can still move). Fusion 360: 7 joint types (Rigid, Revolute, Slider, Cylindrical, Pin-slot, Planar, Ball) plus the distinction between a Joint and an As-built Joint. Onshape (AutoMate): 8 mate types (Fastened, Revolute, Slider, Cylindrical, Pin slot, Planar, Parallel, Ball) plus mate relations (Gear, Rack and pinion, Screw, Linear, according to Onshape's help page; whether all four occur in the AutoMate data is not stated) [uncertain]. Fusion 360 also has 24 hole types (plain, counterbore, countersunk, tapered, blind or through, with conical, spherical or tapered bottoms). Assemble Them All: no type labels, only 'translation-only' versus 'rotational' assembly motion (screw, puzzle, other)
coverage.example_types: rigid (fastened) joint - parts locked together, 0 degrees of freedom; revolute joint (hinge, pin joint) - turn around one axis; slider joint (prismatic joint) - slide along one axis; cylindrical joint - slide and turn on the same axis (like a shaft in a plain bearing); pin-slot joint - turn around a pin that can also slide along a slot; planar joint - slide anywhere on a flat face and turn about its normal; ball joint (spherical joint); parallel mate - faces kept parallel; gear relation - two turning parts coupled at a fixed ratio (Onshape mate relation) [uncertain: presence in data]; rack-and-pinion relation - turning coupled to sliding [uncertain: presence in data]; screw relation - turning coupled to sliding along the same axis (a leadscrew or bolt thread) [uncertain: presence in data]; linear relation - two sliders coupled at a ratio (e.g. telescoping) [uncertain: presence in data]; screw-and-nut assembly motion (Assemble Them All rotational subset); interlocking puzzle assembly (Assemble Them All); counterbore and countersunk bolt holes (Fusion 360 hole labels)
coverage.making_methods: General engineering and product design in CAD (Fusion 360 and Onshape users: robotics, machine design, automotive, toys, product design, according to the Fusion 360 category tags). Aimed at machine learning and robotic assembly research, not at a making method
coverage.item_count: Fusion 360 Gallery Assembly: 8,251 assemblies / 154,468 parts; Assembly-Joint subset: 19,156 joint sets / 32,148 joints / 23,029 parts. AutoMate: 255,211 assemblies / 451,967 unique parts / 1,292,016 unique mates (the paper's cleaned subset: 92,529 top-level assemblies and 541,635 unique mates). Assemble Them All: 12,970 assemblies (8,776 two-part, 2,620 with 3-9 parts, 1,468 with 10-49, 106 with 50-235) plus 24 rotational assemblies. Joint-type vocabulary: 7 (Fusion 360) and 8 (Onshape) types
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: torque-limiting: no; self-locking: no; hand-release only: no; one-way/ratchet: no; indexing/detent: no (joint limits and rest values exist, but no detent behaviour); over-centre: no; compliant: no (all parts are rigid bodies); print-in-place: no; gear trains/gearboxes: only indirectly, through Onshape gear and rack-and-pinion mate relations that couple two joints at a ratio (in the AutoMate schema as 'mateRelations' with a ratio; which relation types occur is not listed) [uncertain]; the gear geometry itself is only present as ordinary parts; powered connectors: no; adhesive types: no. Fasteners appear only as ordinary parts with rigid joints and labelled holes (Fusion 360) and as screw/nut assembly motions (Assemble Them All)
coverage.entry_structure: Per joint: the two parts, the joint type, the designer-selected faces or edges on each part that define the joint, joint axis (origin and direction), offset, angle, flip flag, motion limits (minimum, maximum, rest value) and the transform to the assembled pose. Per assembly: the part hierarchy (tree), occurrences, bodies with material and physical properties, contact faces, labelled holes, user tags (category, industry, products) and a PNG thumbnail. AutoMate: parts, occurrences with 4x4 transforms, mates with type and mate connector frames, mate relations with ratio or length, mate groups and sub-assemblies. No descriptions, design rules or how-to
coverage.audience_level: research (machine learning, computer graphics, robotic assembly planning)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: low. The datasets are large machine-learning archives with JSON and CAD kernel formats and no plain-English explanations. The only beginner-friendly parts are the README diagrams: a figure of the 7 Fusion 360 joint types with their degrees of freedom, and animated GIFs of parts being assembled
usefulness.has_images: yes. Every assembly and joint set has a PNG thumbnail; the READMEs and papers have mosaics of sample assemblies, a diagram of the 7 joint motion types, contact and hole illustrations, and the AutoMate paper has a figure of its 8 mate types with arrows showing the allowed motions. Good quality but small and technical
usefulness.has_animations: yes, limited. Animated GIFs in the JoinABLe README (task, representation and architecture) and Assemble Them All README (parts being disassembled and reassembled along planned paths, including screw-out motions); a GIF showing how a joint is set up in Fusion 360. Assemble Them All includes a simulation viewer that animates assemblies. No interactive web viewer
usefulness.gaps: No clever or special connection types at all: no snap fits, latches, ratchets, detents, torque limiters, compliant joints, print-in-place joints, powered connectors or adhesives. No names in everyday words, no descriptions, no design rules, no guidance on when to use which joint. The type list is only the dozen or so generic CAD joints. The data needs specialist tools, and the Fusion 360 part of it cannot be redistributed or used commercially
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: low. There are no per-item web pages; items are files inside archives, named by IDs (e.g. joint_set_00001.json). The only linkable pages are the repo documentation pages, e.g. https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/Fusion360GalleryDataset/blob/master/docs/assembly_joint.md for the joint-type list [uncertain: exact github.com path, read here via raw.githubusercontent.com], and the Onshape help page on mate relations (https://cad.onshape.com/help/Content/relations.htm)
usefulness.reusable_data: structured. All three are downloadable datasets with documented JSON schemas (AutoMate also has Parquet metadata tables for parts, assemblies and mates), so joint-type counts or example assemblies could be extracted by script. Licence for reuse: AutoMate is CC0 1.0 (free reuse, including the type list and statistics); Fusion 360 Gallery and Assemble Them All data are non-commercial research only and cannot be redistributed in full. The joint-type names themselves are generic CAD vocabulary and can be reused freely
usefulness.maintained: Archived research releases, still online. Fusion 360 Gallery repo and S3 downloads were reachable in September 2026; no new Fusion 360 subsets seen since the 2021-2022 joint release [uncertain]. AutoMate: deposited on Zenodo and Dryad in March 2023 (permanent DOIs), code tagged v1.0.4. Assemble Them All: dataset updated March 2024 (easier custom inputs); dataset links on people.csail.mit.edu listed in the README (not opened). The project website http://assembly.csail.mit.edu/ returned an access error from here [uncertain: whether it is still up]
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Use a short, fixed 'how does it move' vocabulary, based on degrees of freedom, as one flow-chart filter: rigid/fixed, hinge (turns), slider (slides), turn-and-slide (cylindrical), ball (swivels), pin-in-slot, flat-sliding (planar); CAD users already know these words. (2) Show each motion type with the small arrows diagram used in the Fusion 360 and AutoMate figures (translation arrows plus rotation arrows per axis). (3) Record motion limits and a rest position for each entry (e.g. a hinge that opens 0 to 110 degrees). (4) Real-world frequency data: among about 540,000 unique Onshape mates in the AutoMate paper, 62% are rigid (fastened) and only about 1% are ball or pin-slot, which shows that most real joints are fixed and moving joints are the minority. (5) Treat 'coupled motions' (gear, rack-and-pinion, screw relations) as their own group, as Onshape does. (6) Separate 'how it moves' from 'how it is held' (e.g. hole type: counterbore versus countersunk)
usefulness.design_rules_given: No. Only data: contact is defined within a 0.1 mm tolerance, and holes have measured diameters and lengths, but there are no clearances, fits, torques or strength figures
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: No geometry generator for makers. The data come from parametric CAD (Fusion 360 and Onshape B-Reps), and the research code can predict or plan joints (JoinABLe predicts joint axes and poses; AutoMate had an Onshape browser extension that suggests mates; Assemble Them All plans assembly paths), but none of it produces custom connection geometry
usefulness.file_formats: JSON (assembly, joint set and graph data in NetworkX format), SMT (Autodesk Shape Manager B-Rep), STEP, OBJ meshes, PNG thumbnails, Parasolid .x_t (AutoMate), Parquet tables (AutoMate), pickle preprocessed files (JoinABLe); archives are 7z and zip
usefulness.terminology_value: medium. A good authority for the standard CAD names of joint types (revolute, slider, cylindrical, pin-slot, planar, ball, rigid/fastened, parallel) as used in Fusion 360 and Onshape, and for how the two programs name the same thing differently (rigid versus fastened). Useless for names of clever or specialised connections
usefulness.decision_support: None. There is no selector, flow chart or comparison. The only decision-relevant content is the degrees-of-freedom figure for each joint type and the frequency table of mate types
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Fusion 360 Gallery comes from about 20,000 user designs on the Autodesk Online Gallery; its joint types follow the Fusion 360 API. AutoMate is scraped from public Onshape documents and follows Onshape's mate types. Assemble Them All builds mostly on the Fusion 360 Gallery assemblies (Willis et al.), plus assemblies from Ebinger et al. 2018 and puzzle assemblies from Zhang et al. 2020; it shares authors with JoinABLe. The JoinABLe paper compares itself with AutoMate as a concurrent, similar dataset. Overlaps with articulated-object datasets such as PartNet-Mobility/SAPIEN and Shape2Motion, which label hinge, slider and screw joints on everyday objects (cited in both papers); the ABC dataset has Onshape CAD parts but no joints
